subsystems.name: Assembler unit
subsystems.role: a single machine, a few nanometres across, that holds and positions reactive chemical groups so they bond where you want.
parts: rigid molecular frame (e.g. a diamondoid or polymer scaffold)

subsystems.name: Positioning drive
subsystems.role: moves the tool with sub-nanometre precision and applies the force needed to make or break a bond.

subsystems.name: Power supply
subsystems.role: delivers energy to each unit locally, since a wire is impossible.
parts: chemical fuel such as a high-energy bond
or light or an external electric field

subsystems.name: Signalling and coordination
subsystems.role: implements stigmergy: units release marker molecules and sense the gradients left by others, so the swarm organises without central control.

subsystems.name: Instruction and error control
subsystems.role: tells each unit what to build and stops small mistakes compounding.
parts: sequence-defined polymer or DNA strand as program

subsystems.name: Containment
subsystems.role: keeps the swarm where it is wanted — inside a reactor, or inside a body or a spill zone.
parts: immune or environmental compatibility (medical and cleanup use)

buildSteps.title: Design the building block
buildSteps.detail: Chemists specify a rigid molecular framework carrying exactly one reactive tool tip, small enough (roughly 1–10 nm) to work on single bonds.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the unit
buildSteps.detail: Stepwise organic synthesis, or self-assembly of DNA strands into a shaped scaffold, produces identical copies in bulk — as DNA origami already does for static shapes.

buildSteps.title: Add motion and fuel
buildSteps.detail: A molecular motor powered by a chemical fuel, light or an electric field is attached, together with a mechanical limit so it cannot crush what it is building.

buildSteps.title: Give it a voice
buildSteps.detail: Emitter and receptor groups are added so each unit deposits and senses signalling molecules, letting neighbours follow and reinforce a trail rather than needing a controller.

buildSteps.title: Prove one unit works
buildSteps.detail: A single unit, held in place by a scanning probe or a surface, is shown placing atoms in a chosen pattern — the kind of manipulation already done with microscope tips, but automated and repeated.

buildSteps.title: Run many in parallel
buildSteps.detail: Arrays of thousands of identical units work side by side on a surface, since one unit working alone would be hopelessly slow.

buildSteps.title: Add error correction
buildSteps.detail: A proofreading step checks each bond or building block, rejecting and retrying failures so defects do not propagate through the product.

buildSteps.title: Contain and test
buildSteps.detail: First enclosed in a sealed vessel, then in controlled trials for a single task such as capturing a specific pollutant; replication, if used at all, is kept under outside control.

buildSteps.title: Scale manufacture
buildSteps.detail: Units are made by ordinary chemistry or self-assembly in bulk, not by building each one atom by atom — the only route that could ever produce trillions.

prerequisites.why: individual atoms have been positioned and individual reactions driven with scanning probe tips, but not at useful rates, yields or scale; the feasibility of general molecular manufacturing is still debated, notably in the 2003 exchange between Richard Smalley and K. Eric Drexler.
rotary motors and switches won the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, proving molecules can do mechanical work — but no such machine yet builds arbitrary molecules.
DNA nanotechnology builds designed nanometre shapes reliably, giving a possible scaffold and program carrier, though only for a narrow set of structures.
stigmergy is well understood in ant colonies and used in swarm robotics, but chemical signalling between artificial units at trillion-unit density has not been demonstrated.
reactions release heat in nanometre volumes; removing it without damaging the machine is unsolved.

pathway.milestone: probe-based atom manipulation and synthetic molecular motors in laboratories
pathway.unlocks: tools that can touch and move single atoms and molecules.

pathway.milestone: parallel arrays of tips or molecular machines performing the same reaction at thousands of sites at once
pathway.unlocks: realistic throughput for atomically precise surface chemistry.

pathway.milestone: an enclosed demonstrator that follows a stored program and builds a simple target molecule with error checking
pathway.unlocks: proof that programmed molecular construction is possible at all.

pathway.milestone: task-specific swarms for medicine or pollution capture, steered by external fields and local chemical trails
pathway.unlocks: useful work from nanoscale agents without needing general-purpose manufacturing.

pathway.milestone: general molecular manufacturing, if replication, error rates, energy and control can all be solved
pathway.unlocks: materials and medicines built to atomic specification — otherwise the concept stays a research program.
